title: The Hard Part of Dementia Care Isn't the Dementia Patient—It's the Caregiver Who Gets Dragged Down
dek: The difficulty of dementia care lies not in the patient's condition itself, but in the caregivers who are worn down day after day—care turns wives into nurses and forces a post-90s worker to quit. Love is the starting point, but not the support; the system has yet to catch these families.
why: This is not elderly health popular science, but a sociologist's honest fieldwork inside dementia families: no standard answers, only realities you must see before it's too late.
who: Only children born in the 1980s and 1990s, and urbanites whose parents are aging while they have made no elder-care arrangements; also those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care resource gap ultimately falls back on every family
points.body: China has 323 million people aged 60 and above, 23% of the total population; 35 million are disabled elderly, yet there are only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap is not absorbed by the market or institutions; the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patient numbers account for nearly 30% of the global total, and the host estimates that on average, one in every 20 Chinese families is affected—for the first generation of only children, this may be the reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies are unreliable
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, Tang Yong most wants to correct the misconception that dementia patients have a uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia comes mostly from movies, neighbors, or hearsay; the incontinence of the professor in Still Alice is just one form. He met an elderly man who, despite dementia from his tailor background, would still notice stains on visitors' clothes and teach them to remove them with orange peel; and another who, after losing function due to a car accident, would focus intently when humming Liuyang River. Dementia itself covers multiple causes—Alzheimer's, vascular dementia, and others—and each person's life imprint remains in different ways; care cannot follow a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal depends on national care insurance
points.body: Most people see the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: residents shop and go to cafes like ordinary citizens, while staff pose as shopkeepers to maintain a normal atmosphere. But the host adds details that expose its low replicability—the 23 houses built in 2009 cost over 18 million euros, of which 17.8 million was borne by the government, and residents' costs are also covered by long-term care-related systems. In contrast, what Tang Yong saw in a low-income U.S. nursing home was the opposite: elevators had to be locked to prevent dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease differs not in philosophy but in the national payment system.

points.h: Love is not enough; sacrifice can drag down the caregiver
points.body: The host captures the caregiver's predicament well: many swing between 'I love my parents very much' and 'I am about to be dragged down by them.' Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse must learn to bathe, feed, and manage emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a beautifiable devotion: twenty years ago in Guangzhou, he interviewed a daughter who, after caring for her disabled father, divorced and fell into severe depression; the book also features a post-90s caregiver forced to quit due to caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, caregivers themselves become patients.

points.h: The more you see, the less confident you feel about aging
points.body: Having studied elder care for years, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his parents' old age. He is a first-generation only child; his parents are both 75 this year, but the more cases he sees, the less certain he becomes. His research assistant even said after each interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how to arrange her own parents' future. Multi-child families also have friction: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving causes bedsores; only-child families lack shared manpower, and one person who moved parents to Shenzhen found rent, medical costs, and nanny fees piling up faster than retirement wages rose. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child alone.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing someone every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that caregivers must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elderly man who initially could draw blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later could only praise others and dared not put brush to paper; another woman's husband reported new losses every week: his wife could not recognize their daughter's newborn grandson and did not know where this child had come from. This daily, irreversible downward slide drains caregivers more than physical disability. The long haul of care is not repetitive hardship but facing a small farewell every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived, but it doesn't cover every elder
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, and by around 2025 had expanded to about 90 cities; the official pace is to move toward universal coverage in the next two to three years. But Tang Yong reminds that long-term care insurance does not hand out cash to every elder; through unified assessment, it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home care, meal delivery, and other services; those with mild conditions may not qualify. The hardest part is also cultural: sending parents to a nursing home in China is often equated with filial impiety, and elders, like the grandfather in the interview, feel their hair will fall out within a month. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the proportion choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap will not disappear on its own.

quotes.text: I swing back and forth between 'I love my parents very much' and 'I am about to be dragged down by my parents.'

So I think care should still be a kind of relationship. In this relationship, I think both the caregiver and the care recipient undergo great changes in identity, emotions, and even the pace of their lives.
It's like going down a slide—you are on a downward path. So at that moment, I think this kind of care is indeed long and drawn-out.
I think although love is a very important foundation, it should not be the only condition for care. It still requires external resources, including social support, and so on.

Although the more I see and the more cases I encounter, it does not mean I have a very complete or perfect plan for my parents' future care. Precisely because I have seen so many different stories, it actually leaves me with more confusion.
His wife could not recognize the baby her daughter had given birth to—her little grandson. She didn't know where this little child had come from to their home.
He said, 'In that nursing home, I felt that in this one month, my hair was almost all falling out.'
